text: Now that you can create arrays, you need to select parts of them and combine arrays of different shapes. Those are indexing, slicing, and broadcasting.

In one dimension, indexing works like lists. Position zero is the first element, and negative positions count from the end. A slice takes a start, a stop, and a step, and stops just before the stop. You can also index with a list of positions to pick exactly those elements.

Here is the surprise. A basic slice is a view, not a copy. If you change an element through the slice, the original array changes too. When you need a separate array, call dot copy. Selecting with a list of positions or a boolean mask always gives you a copy.

In two dimensions, you give rows first, then columns, separated by a comma. A colon on its own means everything along that dimension. So m of one comma two is a single value, colon comma one is a whole column, and zero to two comma one to three is a block. Boolean masks work here too, and you can assign through them.

Now broadcasting. When shapes differ, NumPy compares them from the rightmost dimension backward. Each pair of sizes must be equal, or one of them must be one. A missing dimension counts as one. Then the ones are stretched to fit, without copying any data.

Multiply a two by three array of order quantities by three unit prices, and the prices are stretched across each row. But add an array of length two, and the last dimensions are three and two, so NumPy raises a ValueError instead of guessing. To fix it, reshape into a column with none inside brackets.
You can now select any part of an array and combine arrays of different shapes. Next lesson: math and statistics with NumPy.
